claim: The opacity of adult brains makes microendoscopy the method of choice for imaging neurons and neural activity in deeply buried brain structures.
source: The opacity of adult brains makes microendoscopy, with an optical probe such as a gradient index (GRIN) lens embedded into brain tissue to provide optical relay, the method of choice for imaging neurons and neural activity in deeply buried brain structures.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about brain imaging methods.

claim: Incorporating a Bessel focus scanning module into two-photon fluorescence microendoscopy extended the excitation focus axially and improved its lateral resolution.
source: Incorporating a Bessel focus scanning module into two-photon fluorescence microendoscopy, we extended the excitation focus axially and improved its lateral resolution.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported by the authors based on their experimental work.

claim: Scanning the Bessel focus in 2D enabled imaging volumes of neurons at high-throughput while resolving fine structures such as synaptic terminals.
source: Scanning the Bessel focus in 2D, we imaged volumes of neurons at high-throughput while resolving fine structures such as synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported by the authors based on their experimental work.

claim: The approach was applied to volumetric anatomical imaging of dendritic spines and axonal boutons in the mouse hippocampus.
source: We applied this approach to the volumetric anatomical imaging of dendritic spines and axonal boutons in the mouse hippocampus, and functional imaging of GABAergic neurons in the mouse lateral hypothalamus in vivo.
evidence: This describes the experimental applications performed by the authors.

claim: The approach was applied to functional imaging of GABAergic neurons in the mouse lateral hypothalamus in vivo.
source: We applied this approach to the volumetric anatomical imaging of dendritic spines and axonal boutons in the mouse hippocampus, and functional imaging of GABAergic neurons in the mouse lateral hypothalamus in vivo.
evidence: This describes the experimental applications performed by the authors.

claim: In brains that strongly scatter light, the image depth of conventional multiphoton microscopy is limited to 1–2 millimeters.
source: In brains that strongly scatter light (i.e., all known adult mammalian brains), the image depth of conventional multiphoton microscopy is limited to 1–2 millimeters (Ji et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: All known adult mammalian brains strongly scatter light.
source: In brains that strongly scatter light (i.e., all known adult mammalian brains), the image depth of conventional multiphoton microscopy is limited to 1–2 millimeters (Ji et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about mammalian brains.

claim: To reach depths beyond a few millimeters, microendoscopy with GRIN lenses is the only practical method currently available.
source: To reach depths beyond a few millimeters, the only practical methods currently available are based on microendoscopy, in which miniature probes, such as gradient refractive index (GRIN) lenses, are embedded within the brain to relay microscopic images of the neurons below (Jung and Schnitzer, 2003; Jung et al., 2004; Levene et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work establishing microendoscopy methods.

claim: Microendoscopy systems have been used for fluorescence activity imaging of neurons expressing genetically encoded calcium indicators in a variety of deep nuclei in the mouse brain.
source: Such systems have been used for fluorescence activity imaging of neurons expressing genetically encoded calcium indicators in a variety of deep nuclei in the mouse brain (Ghosh et al., 2011; Li et al., 2017; Ziv et al., 2013; Bocarsly et al., 2015; Jennings et al., 2015; Kitamura et al., 2015; Pinto and Dan, 2015; Harrison et al., 2016; Okuyama et al., 2016; Kamigaki and Dan, 2017; Kitamura et al., 2017; McHenry et al., 2017; Roy et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The spatial resolution of previous microendoscopy studies has been limited to the cellular level and synaptic structures such as dendritic spines or axonal boutons were not resolved.
source: however, the spatial resolution has been limited to the cellular level and synaptic structures such as dendritic spines or axonal boutons were not resolved in these studies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited previous studies.

claim: Surgeries to remove brain tissue and embed endoscope probes typically have lower success rates compared to conventional craniotomies in which no brain tissue is removed.
source: First, surgeries to remove brain tissue and embed endoscope probes typically have lower success rates compared to conventional craniotomies in which no brain tissue is removed.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about surgical procedures.

claim: Many microendoscopy experiments involve behaviors or brain states with large variability that either cannot be evoked with high fidelity over repeated trials or exhibit short-term adaptation.
source: Second, many microendoscopy experiments involve behaviors or brain states with large variability that either cannot be evoked with high fidelity over repeated trials or exhibit short-term adaptation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about experimental challenges.

claim: Research interests are often centered on specific cell types that are usually sparsely distributed in 3D.
source: Finally, research interests are often centered on specific cell types (e.g., inhibitory subtypes [Pinto and Dan, 2015] or cholinergic neurons [Harrison et al., 2016]) that are usually sparsely distributed in 3D.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and stated as a general observation.

claim: A volumetric microendoscopic imaging method that can simultaneously probe the activity of neural ensembles in 3D while maintaining synapse-resolving spatial resolution has yet to be demonstrated for in vivo volumetric imaging of deep brain structures.
source: For these reasons, a volumetric microendoscopic imaging method, which can simultaneously probe the activity of neural ensembles in 3D while maintaining synapse-resolving spatial resolution, would be greatly beneficial for interrogating neural circuit functions at depth but has yet to be demonstrated for in vivo volumetric imaging of deep brain structures.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the existing literature.

claim: A suite of methods has been developed to image superficial structures at high speed with conventional microscopy.
source: In contrast to the paucity of high-throughput, high-resolution volumetric imaging solutions for microendoscopy, a suite of methods has been developed to image superficial structures at high speed with conventional microscopy (Ji et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Bessel focus scanning combined with two-photon fluorescence microscopy enabled fast volumetric imaging with synaptic resolution in vivo.
source: Recently, we developed a Bessel focus scanning method that, when combined with two-photon fluorescence microscopy (Denk et al., 1990), enabled fast volumetric imaging with synaptic resolution (Lu et al., 2017) in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: By scanning an axially extended focus in two dimensions, projection images of 3D volumes were obtained that increased imaging throughput and reduced data size by 10-to-100-fold.
source: By scanning an axially extended focus in two dimensions (2D), we obtained projection images of 3D volumes that increased imaging throughput and reduced data size by 10-to-100-fold.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' previous work.

claim: The elongation of the focus in the axial direction makes imaging resistant to axial motion artifacts.
source: The elongation of the focus in the axial direction also makes imaging resistant to axial motion artifacts, making it ideally suited to the study of neural circuit functions in awake, behaving animals.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the Bessel focus method.

claim: High-throughput, high-resolution volumetric imaging of neurons and neural activity in deeply buried nuclei is achievable by combining Bessel focus scanning with microendoscopy.
source: Here, we showed that high-throughput, high-resolution volumetric imaging of neurons and neural activity in deeply buried nuclei is achievable by combining Bessel focus scanning with microendoscopy.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported by the authors.

claim: The authors systematically evaluated and identified commercially available GRIN lenses through which high-quality Bessel foci can be generated.
source: We systematically evaluated and identified commercially available GRIN lenses through which high-quality Bessel foci can be generated.
evidence: This describes the experimental work performed by the authors.

claim: Volumetric imaging can be achieved with microendoscopy while maintaining synapse-resolving resolution for anatomical and functional imaging of neurons at depth.
source: We demonstrated in brain slices ex vivo and in the mouse brain in vivo that volumetric imaging can be achieved with microendoscopy while maintaining synapse-resolving resolution for anatomical and functional imaging of neurons at depth.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported by the authors based on their experimental work.

claim: The endoscopy part of the microscope was realized by having a GRIN lens relay the focus of a conventional microscope objective from the image side to the sample side.
source: Based on a standard two-photon excitation fluorescence microscope equipped with a pair of galvo scanners, the endoscopy part of the microscope was realized by having a GRIN lens relay the focus of a conventional microscope objective from the image side to the sample side (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the technical implementation of the microscope system.

claim: Only GRIN lenses with 0.5 mm or 1 mm diameters and a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.5 were considered due to the small size of the mouse brain.
source: Due to the small size of the mouse brain, we only considered GRIN lenses with 0.5 mm or 1 mm diameters and a numerical aperture (NA) of 0.5.
evidence: This describes the experimental design choices made by the authors.

claim: Doublet GRIN lenses have lower intrinsic aberrations than singlets of similar lengths.
source: With part of the GRIN lens assembly having a lower NA, doublet GRIN lenses have lower intrinsic aberrations than singlets of similar lengths.
evidence: This is stated as a property of doublet GRIN lenses based on their optical design.

claim: A 0.45 NA microscope objective was used in conjunction with 0.5-NA singlet GRIN lenses.
source: A 0.45 NA microscope objective was used in conjunction with 0.5-NA singlet GRIN lenses, whereas a 0.2 NA objective was used with doublet GRIN lenses to match their NA on the image side.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used by the authors.

claim: A 0.2 NA objective was used with doublet GRIN lenses to match their NA on the image side.
source: A 0.45 NA microscope objective was used in conjunction with 0.5-NA singlet GRIN lenses, whereas a 0.2 NA objective was used with doublet GRIN lenses to match their NA on the image side.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used by the authors.

claim: GRIN lenses have intrinsic aberrations which limit the resolution and field of view of microendoscopy under the conventional Gaussian mode.
source: GRIN lenses have intrinsic aberrations (Lee and Yun, 2011; Bortoletto et al., 2011), which limit the resolution and field of view (FOV) of microendoscopy under the conventional Gaussian mode (Wang and Ji, 2013; Wang and Ji, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: GRIN lenses with minimal aberrations are required to generate Gaussian and Bessel foci of the highest quality.
source: To generate Gaussian and Bessel foci of the highest quality, GRIN lenses with minimal aberrations are required.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optical properties of GRIN lenses.

claim: A systematic evaluation of the imaging performance of commercially available GRIN lenses had not been undertaken prior to this study.
source: However, a systematic evaluation of the imaging performance of commercially available GRIN lenses had not been undertaken.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the existing literature.

claim: Three GRIN lenses were found to have the best axial FWHM – FOV combinations: a 1-mm-diameter, 8.1-mm-long doublet GRIN lens with 370-µm-diameter FOV, a 0.5-mm-diameter, 9.9-mm-long doublet GRIN lens with 220-µm-diameter FOV, and a 1-mm-diameter, 4.4-mm-long singlet GRIN lens with 510-µm-diameter FOV.
source: Of the ten GRIN lenses tested (Figure 2), three were found to have the best axial FWHM – FOV combinations (green rectangles, Figure 2): a 1-mm-diameter, 8.1-mm-long doublet GRIN lens with 370-µm-diameter FOV ('1 mm doublet', GRIN No. 4); a 0.5-mm-diameter, 9.9-mm-long doublet GRIN lens with 220-µm-diameter FOV ('0.5 mm doublet', GRIN No. 5); and a 1-mm-diameter, 4.4-mm-long singlet GRIN lens with 510-µm-diameter FOV ('1 mm singlet', GRIN No. 6).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' characterization experiments.

claim: For the three best performing GRIN lenses, the axial FWHMs were below 15 µm over most of the sample/image WDs.
source: For all three GRIN lenses, the axial FWHMs were below 15 µm over most of the sample/image WDs, substantially less than the other GRIN lenses tested (but still larger than the diffraction-limited value at 0.5 NA, 6.3 µm, indicating the existence of intrinsic aberrations).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' characterization experiments.

claim: The axial FWHMs of the three best performing GRIN lenses were still larger than the diffraction-limited value at 0.5 NA (6.3 µm), indicating the existence of intrinsic aberrations.
source: For all three GRIN lenses, the axial FWHMs were below 15 µm over most of the sample/image WDs, substantially less than the other GRIN lenses tested (but still larger than the diffraction-limited value at 0.5 NA, 6.3 µm, indicating the existence of intrinsic aberrations).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing measured values to theoretical limits.

claim: A 0.5-mm-diameter, 7.1-mm-long singlet GRIN lens with 310-µm-diameter FOV and an axial FWHM between 18 µm and 32 µm was chosen for further characterization despite having larger aberrations because it had the lowest cost and the largest FOV for 0.5-mm-diameter GRIN lenses.
source: In addition to these best performing lenses, we chose an additional GRIN lens for further characterization, a 0.5-mm-diameter, 7.1-mm-long singlet GRIN lens with 310-µm-diameter FOV and an axial FWHM between 18 µm and 32 µm ('0.5 mm singlet', red rectangle, Figure 2, GRIN No. 10). Even though it had larger aberrations, this GRIN lens had the lowest cost of all GRIN lenses tested and the largest FOV for 0.5-mm-diameter GRIN lenses.
evidence: This describes the experimental design choices made by the authors.

claim: Bessel foci of 0.3 NA had the best performance, yielding higher quality images of fluorescent beads both in the center and towards the edges of the FOV.
source: Applying different binary phase patterns to the SLM in the Bessel module (Lu et al., 2017), we generated axially extended foci of varying NAs and discovered that Bessel foci of 0.3 NA had the best performance, yielding higher quality images of fluorescent beads both in the center and towards the edges of the FOV (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' characterization experiments.

claim: By changing the incident beam size onto the SLM, the axial FWHM of the Bessel focus could be easily adjusted from 40 μm to 120 μm.
source: By changing the incident beam size onto the SLM, the axial FWHM of the Bessel focus could be easily adjusted from 40 μm to 120 μm.
evidence: This describes a technical capability of the system.

claim: 0.3-NA Bessel foci have higher lateral resolution than 0.5-NA Gaussian foci at the center of the FOV.
source: Furthermore, we found 0.3-NA Bessel foci to have higher lateral resolution than 0.5-NA Gaussian foci (Welford, 1960; Sheppard and Wilson, 1979) at the center of the FOV, as indicated by the lateral point spread functions measured from 0.2-µm-diameter fluorescent beads (Figure 4) as well as superior performance when imaging 2-µm-diameter fluorescent beads away from the FOV center (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' characterization experiments, supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Bessel focus scanning improves the lateral resolution at the FOV center while providing a comparable, if not larger, FOV compared to conventional Gaussian imaging.
source: By carefully characterizing the imaging performance of the four selected GRIN lenses, we found that Bessel focus scanning improves the lateral resolution at the FOV center while providing a comparable, if not larger, FOV compared to conventional Gaussian imaging.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the authors' characterization experiments.

claim: For both Bessel and Gaussian modes, if budget and space allow, higher quality GRIN lenses should always be utilized to achieve optimal imaging performance.
source: For both Bessel and Gaussian modes, if budget and space allow, higher quality GRIN lenses should always be utilized to achieve optimal imaging performance.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' findings.

claim: For the 1 mm doublet, a single 2D scan using a 0.3-NA, 68-µm-axial-FWHM Bessel focus captured all 233 interneurons distributed across a 510 µm × 510 µm × 70 µm volume, which required 15 scans of the Gaussian focus to cover.
source: For the 1 mm singlet (Figure 7C,D), a single 2D scan using a 0.3-NA, 68-µm-axial-FWHM Bessel focus captured all 233 interneurons distributed across a 510 µm × 510 µm × 70 µm volume, which required 15 scans of the Gaussian focus to cover (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' experiments in brain tissue.

claim: Bessel focus scanning through the 1 mm singlet imaged a 510 µm × 510 µm × 72 µm volume of somata and neurites of sparsely labeled pyramidal neurons that otherwise required 19 Gaussian 2D planes to image.
source: Similarly and without compromise in lateral resolution, Bessel focus scanning through this same GRIN lens imaged a 510 µm × 510 µm × 72 µm volume of somata and neurites of sparsely labeled pyramidal neurons that otherwise required 19 Gaussian 2D planes to image (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' experiments in brain tissue.

claim: For both 1.0 mm and 0.5 mm doublets, the significantly higher lateral resolution of the 0.3-NA Bessel foci allowed dendritic spines of the pyramidal neurons to be more easily visualized in the Bessel images than in the Gaussian image stacks.
source: For both 1.0 mm and 0.5 mm doublets (Figure 7E–H), the significantly higher lateral resolution of the 0.3-NA Bessel foci allowed dendritic spines of the pyramidal neurons to be more easily visualized in the Bessel images than in the Gaussian image stacks (white arrowheads, Figure 7F,H).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experiments in brain tissue.

claim: Bessel focus scanning improves imaging throughput of two-photon fluorescence microendoscopy by at least 10 × while improving lateral resolution and producing sharper images of synapses in brain tissue.
source: These data demonstrate that Bessel focus scanning improves imaging throughput of two-photon fluorescence microendoscopy by at least 10 × while improving lateral resolution and producing sharper images of synapses in brain tissue.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the authors' experiments in brain tissue.

claim: A polyimide cannula was implanted into brains of Thy1-GFP-M mice to hold the 1 mm doublet GRIN lens above the CA1 region of the hippocampus during imaging sessions.
source: A polyimide cannula (Bocarsly et al., 2015) was implanted into brains of Thy1-GFP-M mice, in order to hold the 1 mm doublet GRIN lens above the CA1 region of the hippocampus during imaging sessions (Figure 8, Figure 9).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used by the authors.

claim: A volume of 370 µm × 370 µm × 53 µm obtained by scanning the Gaussian focus over 14 2D planes was imaged by a single 2D scanning of a Bessel focus (NA = 0.3, axial FWHM = 53 µm) in vivo.
source: A volume of 370 µm × 370 µm × 53 µm obtained by scanning the Gaussian focus over 14 2D planes was imaged by a single 2D scanning of a Bessel focus (NA = 0.3, axial FWHM = 53 µm, Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' in vivo experiments.

claim: Bessel focus scanning provided superior lateral resolution over the Gaussian focus and allowed dendritic spines to be more readily detected in vivo.
source: Similar to the results in the fixed brain slices, all somata and neurites within this volume were imaged by 2D scanning the axially elongated Bessel focus, which also provided superior lateral resolution over the Gaussian focus and allowed dendritic spines to be more readily detected in vivo (cf., white arrowheads, Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' in vivo experiments.

claim: Moving the animal and GRIN lens down by 400 µm shifted the focus upward by 70 µm into a more dorsal layer of the hippocampus.
source: Moving the animal and GRIN lens down by 400 µm shifted the focus upward by 70 µm into a more dorsal layer of the hippocampus, where the structures were dominated by neuronal processes of the CA1 neurons.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure and observation by the authors.

claim: Two-photon fluorescence microendoscopy coupled with the Bessel module is a more advantageous way to image deeply buried albeit sparsely labeled brain structures at synaptic resolution.
source: Combined with the increase of imaging throughput, two-photon fluorescence microendoscopy coupled with the Bessel module is clearly a more advantageous way to image deeply buried albeit sparsely labeled brain structures at synaptic resolution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from their experimental results.

claim: Two-dimensional scanning with a Bessel focus can be used to monitor population activity dynamics of neurons distributed in 3D within deeply buried nuclei in vivo.
source: Two-dimensional scanning with a Bessel focus can also be used to monitor population activity dynamics of neurons distributed in 3D within deeply buried nuclei in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' functional imaging experiments.

claim: The axial extension of the Bessel focus makes the microendoscopic imaging process resistant to axial-motion-induced artifacts.
source: In addition to increased image throughput, the axial extension of the Bessel focus also makes the microendoscopic imaging process resistant to axial-motion-induced artifacts (Lu et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The 0.5 mm singlet GRIN lens was chosen for lateral hypothalamus imaging because it had less insertion damage while providing cellular resolution over a relatively large FOV.
source: With the LH located ~5 mm below the dorsal surface of the brain and our goal of studying cellular-level population activity, we chose to use the 0.5 mm singlet GRIN lens, because it had less insertion damage while providing cellular resolution over a relatively large FOV.
evidence: This describes the experimental design choices made by the authors.

claim: The lateral hypothalamus is located approximately 5 mm below the dorsal surface of the brain.
source: With the LH located ~5 mm below the dorsal surface of the brain and our goal of studying cellular-level population activity, we chose to use the 0.5 mm singlet GRIN lens, because it had less insertion damage while providing cellular resolution over a relatively large FOV.
evidence: This is stated as anatomical knowledge about the mouse brain.

claim: The same neurons could be identified and tracked across sessions both in Gaussian stacks and Bessel images for each mouse, despite recordings being taken during different experimental sessions that were hours and days apart with mice freely behaving in between.
source: Although the neuronal recordings were taken during different experimental sessions that were hours and days apart with mice freely behaving in between, the same neurons could be identified and tracked across sessions both in Gaussian stacks and Bessel images for each mouse (Figure 10A,B).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' functional imaging experiments.

claim: GABAergic neurons in the lateral hypothalamus exhibited frequent, mostly synchronous activity during both ends of light and dark cycles.
source: We found that these GABAergic neurons exhibited frequent, mostly synchronous activity during both ends of light and dark cycles, as indicated by representative traces of calcium transients from selected neurons (Figure 10C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' functional imaging experiments.

claim: When mice were imaged at the end of light cycles, increased activity was observed in lateral hypothalamic GABAergic neurons.
source: When mice were imaged at the end of light cycles, we observed increased activity, which was corroborated by quantitative analysis using the calcium transients from all detected neurons (Figure 10E,G).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' functional imaging experiments.

claim: For both mice, the population activity and synchrony of GABAergic neurons in the lateral hypothalamus increased significantly from the end of dark cycles to the end of light cycles, that is from a satiety-like state to a hunger-like state.
source: For both mice, the population activity and synchrony of these GABAergic neurons increased significantly from the end of dark cycles to the end of light cycles, that is from a satiety-like state to a hunger-like state (175 neurons, 3820 correlation coefficients, non-paired t-test, Figure 10I–K).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' functional imaging experiments with statistical analysis.

claim: 2D Bessel focus scanning microendoscopy enables high-throughput, simultaneous 3D imaging and subsequent analysis of population dynamics in deeply buried brain structures.
source: As demonstrated in this example, 2D Bessel focus scanning microendoscopy enables high-throughput, simultaneous 3D imaging and subsequent analysis of population dynamics in deeply buried brain structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn by the authors from their functional imaging experiments.

claim: Volumetric imaging of neurons and neuronal activity at high spatial and temporal resolution is crucial to study information processing of neuronal circuits.
source: Volumetric imaging of neurons and neuronal activity at high spatial and temporal resolution is crucial to study information processing of neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neuroscience research needs.

claim: Deeply buried brain nuclei can now be accessed optically via microendoscopy through micro-optical probes embedded in the brain.
source: Deeply buried brain nuclei can now be accessed optically via microendoscopy through micro-optical probes embedded in the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about current imaging capabilities.

claim: For structures such as hippocampus and dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus, a cannula with a glass bottom can be embedded to provide optical access after the removal of overlying tissue, and a microscope objective with a long working distance can be used for imaging.
source: For structures such as hippocampus and dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (Mizrahi et al., 2004; Dombeck et al., 2010; Marshel et al., 2012), a cannula with a glass bottom can be embedded to provide optical access after the removal of overlying tissue, and a microscope objective with a long working distance can be used for imaging.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: To image the lateral hypothalamus, which is 5 mm from the top surface of the mouse brain, passing the light cone of a 0.5-NA microscope objective requires 22 mm3 of brain tissue to be removed, whereas an embedded 0.5-mm-diameter GRIN lens only displaces 1 mm3 of brain tissue.
source: For example, to image the lateral hypothalamus, which is 5 mm from the top surface of the mouse brain, passing the light cone of a 0.5-NA microscope objective requires 22 mm3 of brain tissue to be removed, whereas an embedded 0.5-mm-diameter GRIN lens only displaces 1 mm3 of brain tissue.
evidence: This is a calculation based on optical geometry.

claim: Microendoscopy employing GRIN lenses is the preferred method for imaging deep nuclei of the brain.
source: Therefore, microendoscopy employing GRIN lenses is the preferred method for imaging deep nuclei of the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of tissue damage between methods.

claim: Care must be taken to ensure that inflammation has abated before imaging starts and that the physiology of the structures of interest is minimally affected by tissue removal or displacement.
source: In both cases, care must be taken to ensure that inflammation has abated before imaging starts and that the physiology of the structures of interest is minimally affected by tissue removal or displacement.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration.

claim: Existing implementation of microendoscopy suffers from low resolution and/or low throughput.
source: Existing implementation of microendoscopy suffers from low resolution and/or low throughput.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: The intrinsically higher lateral resolution of Bessel foci allowed the authors to resolve dendritic spines and axonal boutons both ex vivo and in vivo.
source: The intrinsically higher lateral resolution of Bessel foci allowed us to resolve dendritic spines and axonal boutons both ex vivo and in vivo, while improving imaging throughput up to 19×.
evidence: This is a summary of the authors' findings.

claim: Bessel focus scanning improved imaging throughput up to 19×.
source: The intrinsically higher lateral resolution of Bessel foci allowed us to resolve dendritic spines and axonal boutons both ex vivo and in vivo, while improving imaging throughput up to 19×.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' experiments.

claim: The axially extended two-photon fluorescence excitation in Bessel focus scanning microendoscopy makes the imaging process immune to axial motion artifacts.
source: The axially extended two-photon fluorescence excitation in Bessel focus scanning microendoscopy also makes the imaging process immune to axial motion artifacts and allowed us to obtain high-quality functional imaging data from awake behaving mice without having to resort to complex post-processing.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' functional imaging experiments.

claim: Because more energy is distributed in the side rings of a Bessel focus, the average power of the excitation light was increased by 1.5–4×, which remains within the safe range for two-photon fluorescence microscopy.
source: Because more energy is distributed in the side rings of a Bessel focus, the average power of the excitation light was increased by 1.5–4×, which remains within the safe range for two-photon fluorescence microscopy (Podgorski and Ranganathan, 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' experiments, supported by a citation about safety limits.

claim: Bessel focus scanning microendoscopy can be applied to more densely labeled samples, and computational methods can be used to demix activity from overlapping neurons.
source: Although we only demonstrated the applications in relatively sparsely labeled samples, Bessel focus scanning microendoscopy can also be applied to more densely labeled samples, and computational methods (Liu et al., 2012; Pnevmatikakis et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2018) can be used to demix activity from overlapping neurons.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications, supported by citations to computational methods.

claim: Bessel focus scanning modules can be added to existing microendoscopy setups without additional changes in data acquisition software.
source: Finally, because Bessel focus scanning modules (Lu et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2018) can be added to existing microendoscopy setups without additional changes in data acquisition software, we expect this method to be easily adoptable for high-throughput synaptic resolution volumetric imaging of deep brain structures.
evidence: This is stated as a technical feature of the method, supported by citations.

claim: The method is expected to be easily adoptable for high-throughput synaptic resolution volumetric imaging of deep brain structures.
source: Finally, because Bessel focus scanning modules (Lu et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2018) can be added to existing microendoscopy setups without additional changes in data acquisition software, we expect this method to be easily adoptable for high-throughput synaptic resolution volumetric imaging of deep brain structures.
evidence: This is speculation about future adoption of the method.

claim: All animal experiments were conducted according to the United States National Institutes of Health guidelines for animal research.
source: All animal experiments were conducted according to the United States National Institutes of Health guidelines for animal research.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental procedures and ethics compliance.

claim: Procedures and protocols were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute.
source: Procedures and protocols were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Janelia Research Campus, Howard Hughes Medical Institute.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental procedures and ethics compliance.

claim: 940 nm output from a femtosecond pulsed laser source was used to provide two-photon excitation.
source: 940 nm output from a femtosecond pulsed laser source with a built-in dispersion compensation unit (InSight DeepSee, Spectra Physics, CA, USA) was used to provide two-photon excitation.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup used by the authors.

claim: Only the thin layer of tissue right next to the implant site exhibited enhanced staining for GFAP.
source: In the example brain (Figure 9), only the thin layer of tissue right next to the implant site exhibited enhanced staining for GFAP, in agreement with a previous study (Bocarsly et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' histological analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: Nissl staining showed some tissue deformation in the hippocampal structures below the implant site.
source: Nissl staining showed some tissue deformation in the hippocampal structures below the implant site.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' histological analysis.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons within the imaging FOV maintained laminar distribution despite tissue deformation.
source: However, CA1 pyramidal neurons within the imaging FOV (indicated by the green bars in Figure 9) maintained laminar distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' histological analysis.

claim: The GFP+ dendrites and axons in the imaged region had normal morphology and were devoid of signs of cell death.
source: This is consistent with the in vivo imaging results in Figure 8 (same brain as in Figure 9), in which the GFP+ dendrites and axons were found to have normal morphology and were devoid of signs of cell death (e.g., fragmented axons).
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' in vivo imaging experiments.

claim: The measured lateral FWHMs of the Bessel foci (0.93–1.27 µm) were similar to their diffraction-limited value (1.06 µm).
source: As a result, we found the measured lateral FWHMs of the Bessel foci (0.93–1.27 µm, Figure 4) to be similar to their diffraction-limited value (1.06 µm) (Richards and Wolf, 1959)
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' characterization experiments, compared to theoretical values.

claim: The lateral resolution of the Gaussian foci (measured FWHMs: 1.02–1.47 µm, diffraction-limited value: 0.78 µm) were substantially degraded by aberrations.
source: whereas the lateral resolution of the Gaussian foci (measured FWHMs: 1.02–1.47 µm, Figure 4, diffraction-limited value: 0.78 µm) were substantially degraded by aberrations.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' characterization experiments, compared to theoretical values.

claim: The circular symmetry of spherical aberrations made them minimally degrade the imaging quality of the Bessel focus formed by annular illumination.
source: The circular symmetry of spherical aberrations made them minimally degrade the imaging quality of the Bessel focus formed by annular illumination.
evidence: This is an inference about the optical properties of Bessel foci.
